top_title: TOP PROBLEMS 3rd Version: all sources side by side (2026-11-04)
top_intro: The Top four problems 2nd Version is unchanged. That version was built from forums, YouTube and papers, and said "Reddit was blocked." This version adds two kinds of Reddit research: (1) a random sample of 500 posts with no keyword filter, coded with the same 14 themes as the forum research, so the numbers can be compared ({N} were written by caregivers), and (2) the 672 caregiver posts about tools and needs from 2026-11-03. Numbers read as main topic / mentioned anywhere. Not a ranking and not a choice: the owner picks the problem.
top_columns: Reddit posts about tools and needs (672)
top_rows: 1. Burnout, guilt, isolation, grief
{Burnout, guilt, isolation, grief}
Doing it alone, family won't help 110; burnout with no one who understands 30; no respite 16
Not a topic in app reviews. AARP/NAC 2025: 24% feel alone; 30% want help managing stress (p.53). Alzheimer's Association 2026: 59% of dementia caregivers report high emotional stress (p.55).
Confirmed as the top problem in every source. On Reddit it's the main topic of 1 in 4 posts and comes up in half.
2. Money, accounts and legal papers
10 (9%) / 39 (33%); logins or accounts in 17
{Money, insurance, legal papers}
Getting into the parent's accounts 132 (banks refuse 46, lost passwords 32, codes to the parent's phone 22); documents and POA 97 (POA missing or rejected 29, papers scattered 22)
App reviews: access for another person 14 of 192 problem reviews. JMIR 2025: 49% of US adults have had digital proxy duties. AARP/NAC: 26% need help with paperwork (p.52).
Confirmed and stronger. Second most mentioned theme in the Reddit sample. The tool posts show the exact blocks: banks, passwords, sign-in codes, POA.
3. Choosing, placing and paying for care
{Choosing, placing and paying for care}
Not measured (the tool posts were sorted by 8 tool features)
Not a topic in app reviews.
Confirmed but a little lower. The old "biggest problem (21 sources)" came from the unsaved NotebookLM summary. Neither the forums nor the Reddit sample show it as biggest.
4. Family coordination and siblings
{Family coordination, siblings}
Siblings won't share the work 63; information spread across chats, calendars and paper 32; updates lost or ignored in group chats 28
App reviews: relatives can't see the same information 7 of 192. AARP/NAC: 53% have unpaid help (p.25). NHATS: about three quarters of older adults get help from one child.
Same pattern in both sources: rarely the main topic, but mentioned in 1 in 4. Reddit shows the core problem is siblings not helping, more than missing information.
5. Dementia behavior and communication
{Dementia behavior and communication}
Not measured
Alzheimer's Association 2026: 48% of caregivers of older adults care for someone with dementia (p.49). AARP/NAC: 12% want help with challenging behaviors (p.53).
Lower on Reddit than in the forums (one forum, ALZConnected, is a dementia community), but still mentioned in about 1 in 4 posts. Stays on the list.
6. The person refuses help (NEW to this list)
{Care recipient refuses help}
Parent forgets or refuses medications 25; parent won't wear the alert device 11
Competitor reviews: Lively is hard for the older person to use (13); Medical Guardian parents stop wearing it (5).
New. The second most common main topic among the named themes in the Reddit sample, much higher than in the forums. It also explains why tools fail: the parent won't use them.
7. Medications
{Medications}
77 posts (medication changes not shared 24; parent forgets or refuses 25)
App reviews: reminders failing 3 of 192. AARP/NAC: 55% do medical or nursing tasks, only 22% were trained (p.34).
Lower as a main topic on Reddit. When it comes up, the risk is changes not being shared (near double doses).
8. Safety and knowing a parent is OK
{Safety}
59 posts (no way to know the parent is OK 19; won't wear the device 11)
App reviews: wrong readings or location 43 and danger with the tool not helping 19, of 192 (mostly two apps the team chose). AARP/NAC: remote monitoring use rose from 13% to 25% (p.37).
Similar to the forums. Families want alerts to reach them.
9. Doctors, appointments, records
{Doctors, appointments, records}
67 posts (too many portals or proxy blocked 25; doctors' offices don't share 16)
AARP/NAC: 64% talk with providers, only 58% find coordinating easy (p.35-36).
Similar: rarely the main topic, mentioned in about 1 in 5.
10. Hands-on personal care, equipment and supplies (NEW)
Not a forum theme
{HANDS_ON} posts as main topic (found in Other)
Not measured
AARP/NAC: 55% do medical or nursing tasks, only 22% were trained (p.34).
New from Reddit: incontinence, bedbound hygiene, wound care, lifting, finding equipment and supplies.
11. The caregiver's own life (job, money, health)
{The caregiver's own life}
Not measured
Not a topic in app reviews.
Similar: rarely the main topic, but mentioned in about 1 in 4.

opp_question: What market segment has the largest opportunity? Why? (updated 2026-11-04, DRAFT for the owner)
opp_answer:
The template's three tests are: big enough, few competitors, and a need that isn't fully met. Here's what Reddit changes for each segment it touches.

• Segment 10, digital vaults and emergency access (the parent's accounts and papers): the unmet-need test is now passed more clearly than any other software segment. Money, insurance and legal papers is the second most mentioned theme ({Money, insurance, legal papers}). In the tool posts, 132 are about getting into the parent's accounts (banks refuse the caregiver 46, lost passwords 32, codes go to the parent's phone 22). Competitive Analysis 2 shows no competitor covers banks or insurers, and MyChart proxy access is hard to get. Against: the size figure is for all password managers ($3.1B to $3.75B), not caregivers. Much of the block is bank and legal policy a family can't change. It has the highest security and liability risk.

• Segment 12, caregiver mental health and burnout: the biggest need in every source ({Burnout, guilt, isolation, grief}), but it fails "few competitors" (Calm, Headspace and other general apps). On Reddit the problem is people not helping, not a missing app.

• Segment 1, family care-coordination apps: confidence stays LOW. Family coordination is the main topic of {Family coordination, siblings}, about the same as the forums. The core complaint is siblings not helping (63 tool posts), and the competitors share news but don't get relatives to act. Caregivers rarely name these apps.

• Segment 4, choosing and paying for care: real ({Choosing, placing and paying for care}), but not the biggest need. The old "biggest problem (21 sources)" came from the unsaved NotebookLM summary. One fee-funded company still dominates.

• Segment 6, remote monitoring: the family side fails (Competitive Analysis 2: Lively works 36, problems 100), but the market is crowded and depends on devices.

Reading (Claude's, not a decision): by the three tests, segment 10 now has the strongest evidence of an unmet need among the software segments. Segment 12 has the biggest need but is crowded. Segment 1 stays low. The owner chooses.
